Stocks broaden out: smaller and debt-heavy companies benefit most

active.title: Oil gets expensive
active.first: Petrol, jet fuel, diesel and plastics cost more within weeks.
active.second: Airlines, truckers and chemical makers see margins squeezed; households spend more on fuel and less on everything else. Inflation readings rise, so the Fed is slower to cut.
active.long_run: Sustained high prices pay for new drilling (more supply later) and speed the shift to EVs, efficiency and renewables - which is why oil spikes tend to undo themselves over 1-2 years.

library.title: The Fed cuts rates
library.first: Short-term borrowing costs and savings rates fall.
library.second: Mortgage rates ease and housing activity picks up; floating-rate borrowers (small companies, private-equity-owned firms) get relief; the dollar tends to weaken, lifting US multinationals' overseas earnings.
library.long_run: Cheaper money encourages risk-taking - more IPOs, more speculation, more borrowing. If cuts come too early, inflation can return (the 1970s pattern).

library.title: Inflation won't come down
library.first: Prices keep rising faster than the Fed's 2% goal; wages chase them.
library.second: Companies that can raise prices without losing customers (strong brands, must-have software, monopolies) protect margins; companies that can't (low-margin retail, restaurants, contractors) get squeezed. The Fed holds rates high.
library.long_run: Expectations shift: workers demand bigger raises, companies raise prices pre-emptively - the hardest kind of inflation to stop, and the reason the Fed reacts strongly to early signs.

library.title: The job market weakens
library.first: Hiring slows, then layoffs rise; people feel less secure.
library.second: Spending on extras (travel, eating out, new cars) is cut first; credit-card and auto-loan losses rise at lenders; wage growth slows, which cools services inflation and lets the Fed cut.
library.long_run: Unemployment tends to rise in a self-reinforcing way once it starts - which is why the 'Sahm rule' (a 0.5-point rise) has called every recession since 1970.

library.title: Tariffs and trade barriers
library.first: Imported goods and parts cost more; trading partners often retaliate.
library.second: Importers and retailers choose between raising prices (inflation) and eating the cost (lower margins); manufacturers using imported parts (autos, machinery) pay more; exporters lose foreign sales to retaliation (farm products, aircraft).
library.long_run: Supply chains move - to Mexico, Vietnam, India, or back to the US. That takes years and builds factories, warehouses and automation, but leaves goods structurally more expensive.

library.title: The AI spending boom
library.first: Big tech companies spend hundreds of billions a year on data centres and chips.
library.second: Chipmakers, memory makers and network gear sellers book record sales; data centres need huge amounts of power, so utilities, grid equipment, cooling and copper demand rise; software companies worry AI tools replace their products.
library.long_run: Either AI earns back the spending - productivity rises across the economy - or spending gets cut, and the suppliers who grew fastest fall hardest. Electricity prices for everyone may rise either way.

library.title: The dollar strengthens
library.first: US goods get more expensive abroad; imports get cheaper at home.
library.second: US multinationals earn less when foreign sales are converted back to dollars; countries and companies that borrowed in dollars find debts harder to repay; commodity prices (priced in dollars) tend to fall.
library.long_run: Persistent strength widens the trade deficit and draws political pressure (tariffs, calls for a weaker dollar).

library.title: Borrowing gets harder
library.first: Lenders demand higher interest from riskier companies, or stop lending.
library.second: Weaker companies can't refinance and cut jobs and investment; private-equity-owned firms and private credit funds come under strain; banks tighten lending standards, slowing the whole economy.
library.long_run: A default cycle clears out weak firms over 1-2 years; survivors gain share. Credit has led stocks at most major turning points.

library.title: Big government deficits
library.first: The Treasury borrows more, selling more bonds.
library.second: To absorb all those bonds, investors demand higher long-term yields; mortgages and corporate borrowing follow them up. Spending itself boosts the industries it targets (defense, infrastructure, subsidised energy).
library.long_run: Interest on the debt grows into one of the largest budget items, crowding out other spending; worries about debt sustainability support gold and pressure the dollar.

model.outlook: The data leans toward a soft landing, because inflation is cooling and the risk appetite is cautious while the Fed’s policy rate is only modestly restrictive. The strongest reason is the drop in core PCE inflation to just above 3% and the modest rise in unemployment, which together suggest slower price pressures. The single thing that would most change the picture is a sharp move in the 2‑year Treasury yield away from the current 4.83% level.

soft_landing.from_here: If inflation continues to cool and the Fed holds rates steady, growth can stay above 1.5% and corporate earnings stay stable, supporting tech valuations. The market would see lower volatility and modest equity gains.
soft_landing.tipping_point: Core PCE 3‑month annualised falling below 2.5% for two consecutive months.

running_hot.from_here: If wages rise faster than expected and core inflation rebounds above 3%, the Fed may raise rates further, tightening financing for high‑growth tech firms. Equity valuations could compress as discount rates climb.
running_hot.tipping_point: Core PCE 3‑month annualised rising above 3% for two months.

stagflation.from_here: If growth slows while inflation stays above 3%, real wages fall and consumer spending contracts, hurting both consumer‑tech and industrials. Credit spreads would widen, raising borrowing costs.
stagflation.tipping_point: Real 10‑year Treasury yield exceeding 3% plus core CPI staying above 2.5%.

downturn.from_here: If hiring drops sharply and unemployment climbs above 4.5%, demand for tech products could fall, leading to earnings cuts and a broader market decline. Liquidity could tighten as banks become more cautious.
downturn.tipping_point: Initial jobless claims rising above 260,000 for two weeks.
